extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; literary scholars and general readers seeking an introduction to The Spectator (Addison & Steele)
extracted.subtask_description: An editorial introduction to The Spectator explaining its historical importance, the characters and temperaments of Addison and Steele, and the literary standards and tastes the work embodies. Useful for readers learning how the essays were shaped and what qualities were valued in early-18th-century English prose and humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning, wit, and humanity as essential merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's wish that the work were 'as honorary to that sacred name as learning, wit, and humanity render those pieces which I have taught the reader how to distinguish for his.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor presents 'learning, wit, and humanity' as core qualities that render essays honourable and memorable. Works aimed at moral instruction or public influence should combine erudition, intellectual vivacity, and humane feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sportive humour: delicately whimsical and gaily wise
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator's humour is described as 'sportive humour, delicately whimsical and gaily wise, which made his conversation the delight of the few men with whom he sat at ease.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comic writing/essays should be gently playful — whimsical yet wise — producing charm without coarse wit. Humour works best when it is light, civilizing, and affable rather than aggressive or merely satirical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious earnestness underpins moral authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeatedly: Addison and Steele had 'religious earnestness' and this earnestness formed 'the deep foundations of this friendship' and of the book (the 'Monument').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral/religious seriousness is presented as a virtue that gives weight and sincerity to essays and humour; it legitimizes ethical criticism and lends lasting value to literary pieces. Writers should couple wit with genuine moral feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy with the whole nation / popular appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's 'sympathies were with all England' and the Spectator is presented as speaking 'for the people and looked to the people for approval and support.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful periodical writing should address broad public sympathies and sensibilities, not only the tastes of an elite. A tone that reaches and sympathizes with 'all England' increases influence and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural thought and speech versus affected French manner
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction contrasts the 'imported Latin style adapted to the taste of patrons' with 'natural thought and speech' and praises breaking from the 'critic[s] of France' who enforced a polished but artificial style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clarity, natural phrasing, and native linguistic resources (Anglo-Saxon elements) over affected, foreign-influenced pedantry. Authentic, natural expression is valued over ornate conformity to foreign critical fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical models but adapt to English roots
rubrics_metrics.description: While Boileau and Latin models influenced critics, the essay argues writers should seek strength by looking to the true sources of English (Saxon) rather than slavishly following Latin/French models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical learning and models are useful, but writers should adapt classical principles to English idiom and sensibility; the aim is harmony and strength suited to the national language rather than imitation for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive classical quotation and scholarly overdosing
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison's foreign travel notes are said to be 'crammed his pages with quotation from Virgil and Horace... and gave even to his 'understanding age' an overdose of its own physic for all ills of literature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overuse of learned quotations or classical allusion can alienate readers and mask original observation. Use classical references sparingly so that they illuminate rather than overwhelm the writer's own voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance seriousness and playfulness (humour veiled, not crushed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor notes Addison's 'humour that was veiled, not crushed' and contrasts Steele's direct warmth; both seriousness and play are combined in successful essays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good essaying/humour blends earnest moral purpose with playful expression — neither should dominate to the exclusion of the other. Humour may be subtle (veiled) while retaining moral seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid didacticism; didactic manner is an anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's 'Christian Hero' is critiqued as 'too didactic' — 'the book was too didactic... plain truth out of Steele's heart, but an air of superiority... belongs to a too didactic manner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral instruction should not become heavy-handed preaching. Writers should teach by example, sympathy, and wit rather than by moralizing with an air of superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use criticism to amend bad taste; the critic's corrective role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator (and its authors) are credited with a 'critical taste' that amended contemporary tastes and 'brought natural thought and speech to their perfection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical writing should seek to correct and refine public taste through reasoned argument and exemplary writing, not merely through fashion or snobbish dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence and tact when addressing patrons or political matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison's use of flattering dedicatory addresses to secure patrons (Somers, Montagu) and his prudence in political/patronage contexts are discussed as practical necessities of a literary career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking patronage or addressing political figures, tact and prudence are practical virtues; writers may temper public expression to maintain support and livelihood without wholly sacrificing integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/political sympathy as basis for literary judgement (e.g., praise of Milton)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison's praise of Milton is tied to 'strong sympathy with [Milton's] high purpose' and the religious/moral dimension of poetry: 'from its religious side... he first entered into the perception of its grandeur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of poetry and serious literature should consider the moral or high purpose behind a work; moral sympathy can be a legitimate ground for critical admiration as well as aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of personal character enriches humour and essays
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's open-hearted sympathy, readiness to give honour to others, and personal warmth are cited as sources of the Spectator's charm: 'Steele wholly comes out of himself... his whole thought on the worth of his companion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A writer's genuine personal character — warmth, generosity, authentic sympathy — enhances the persuasive and comic power of essays; affectation undermines this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fashionable pedantry; prefer service to the public over courtly polish
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor contrasts the 'way of patronage' (polished, fit for select audience) with the 'rough up-hill track' of serving the people; Addison initially followed patronage while Steele chose the popular route.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing aimed chiefly at courtly taste or fashionable pedantry risks irrelevance; serving a wider public, even if rougher, can lead to greater cultural impact and democratic literary value.
